div.p: Embedded computer system architectures are distributed, layered and heterogeneous. Development progresses through a series of model refinements with varying levels of detail in different subsystems. Different requirements models and scheduling methods are used for different functions and equipment. Today there is no single schedulability tool that can analyze all of them. This paper describes an open compositional timing analysis framework that allows developers to select a set of analysis tools suited for the different kinds of subsystems in their product lines. The framework compositionally applies the tools so that dependencies between subsystems are taken into account when producing an overall end-to-end timing analysis.

div.head: I. MODELING EMBEDDED SYSTEMS
div.p: There is strong desire for improved early-phase modelbased development methods. For example, studies have shown that much project cost and schedule overrun is due to rework during integration phases that can be traced back to mistakes in the early requirements and specification phases [27], [7]. However, the use of schedulability analysis for real-world systems is still limited, due in part to the limited capabilities of any single analysis tool relative to the complexities of an entire system. In the following paragraphs we discuss requirements for schedulability analysis of distributed, heterogeneous, layered computer systems in a multi-phase development process.

We selected as our input modeling language the Architecture Analysis and Design Language (AADL) [21]. This is an SAE standard, which supports our openness goals. AADL was developed to support a variety of analyses as well as implementation and verification, and a number of analysis tools exist [1].

The modeling language and tools must support specification of derived computer system timing requirements and their decomposition into timing requirements for subsystems and components. Computer system timing requirements apply to event and data streams that arrive and depart through the interface between the computer system and the physical environment, e.g. the A/D and D/A interfaces within sensors and actuators. These requirements involve complex multi-disciplinary evaluations and trade-offs based on physical sciences and human factors as well as computer science and engineering. AADL provides a "flow" declaration that allows users to identify flows of data and events and their associated timing requirements, both system end-to-end flows and subsystem and component sub-flows.

The modeling language and tools must support a variety of task and message timing models and protocols. For example, feed-back control applications use periodic tasking combined with a sampled data communication protocol that provides distributed state vector update semantics. Communications applications often use event-driven tasking combined with a communications protocol that permits message queuing. Client-server protocols between applications are now appearing in embedded systems (a common web design pattern) in addition to publish-subscribe and shared memory protocols (more traditional in embedded real-time systems). Some applications assume asynchronous event arrivals and departures (e.g. many human/machine interfaces are specified as eventdriven functions). Others may require synchronized inputs (e.g. some navigation applications) or synchronized outputs (e.g. some feed-back control and digital audio applications). Different synchronization requirements are met using different design patterns (e.g. time-triggered, event-triggered, quasisynchronous). Systems use combinations (e.g. Globally Asynchronous Locally Synchronous, GALS). The AADL standard includes a variety of pre-declared properties for common timing models and protocols, and AADL allows tool-specific properties to be defined and used if needed.

The modeling language and tools must support layered architectures. Figure 1 illustrates layering in a complex system. On compute modules, layers of infrastructure software such as real-time operating systems and communications middleware create virtual operating environments with varying Application Program Interfaces (APIs). AADL provides a "virtual processor" construct to declare these. Communication between two software applications builds on layers of network protocols. AADL provides a "virtual bus" construct to declare these. AADL declarations used to specify bindings and routings of software workloads to processor and bus resources (explicitly or as constraints to be satisfied by automated binding and routing tools) may be similarly layered.

The modeling language and tools must support mixedfidelity modeling. Mixed fidelity modeling is often done to limit modeling and analysis time and effort to parts of the system that are novel, or to focus on areas of uncertainty and risk, or to focus on aspects to which requirements are more sensitive. Design detail sufficient for schedulability analysis may only be available for some components. Modeling detail may also be omitted due to intellectual property restrictions. AADL allows interfaces to be declared separately from implementations. Timing interface properties can be used to declare event departure stream models, constraints on event arrival streams, and flow-through latencies. This is illustrated It must be possible to perform at least some analysis on abstract and partial models, including analysis and management of uncertainties and sensitivities. Models progress during development from high-level requirements to detailed implementation. Models capture what should be known given what can be known at any particular milestone, limited by time and effort and uncertainty. Models are elaborated as more information becomes available and more decisions are made. For example, it is common to specify workload demand and supply budgets during the early phases of development (e.g. MIPS, BPS, Bytes), with traceability and analysis to manage compliance of evolving detailed models with those budgets. AADL has refinement and extension features that support evolutionary development of models.

div.head: II. PREVIOUS WORK
div.p: The range of methods that have been applied to allocate, route and schedule software workloads on digital hardware resources is too broad to cite any reasonably comprehensive surveys. The two most common approaches to modeling and analysis of timing performance are simulation and schedulability analysis.

This paper focuses on schedulability analysis. Its strengths (relative to simulation) are that it provides guarantees for all possible behaviors of the model, and models can be concise Fig. 2. Some components only have interface specifications and easily built and quickly solved. Its weaknesses are that theory only exists for some patterns and protocols, and tractable bounds may be loose (overly conservative). Many methods have been developed. Some common examples are busy period (a.k.a. time demand) analysis [13], [10]; network calculi [5], [2]; timed Petri nets [24]; and timed and hybrid automata [25], [8], [16]. These many theories have led to many tools; we are aware of over a dozen available commercially or from universities.

Our approach is to create a framework that allows existing schedulability analysis tools to be applied compositionally. Different parts of a system model are marked to be analyzed by tools appropriate for each. The framework orchestrates the process of dividing the system model for analysis by different tools and recombining the results into an end-to-end system analysis. We have named this the Framework for Analysis of Schedulability, Timing And Resources (FASTAR).

Compositional1 approaches to schedulability analysis have been developed earlier [10], [19], [26]. Previous tools have shown the approach to be feasible and scalable in practice, but they used analysis modules based on the same underlying theory and designed to work together [11], [17], [20]. Composing analysis methods based on different theories and implemented in different tools by different suppliers is still a subject of research [14]. Our goal is an open framework that allows a diverse set of third-party analysis tools to be integrated and used compositionally, where the intellectual property of the different analyzers can be preserved by the different tool developers as they desire.

We do not expect to support an arbitrary mixing and matching of architecture patterns and analyzers. The system architect must carefully choose a set of patterns and protocols that satisfy the overall system requirements and are consistent with each other and available analysis methods. Poor specification of architecture patterns, layers and interfaces in early phases of development, and the resulting incompatibilities between delivered components, is a significant cause of expensive rework during software and system integration [27], [7]. The system architect is expected to reasonably match selected architecture patterns and protocols with available analysis methods.

div.head: III. COMPOSITIONAL SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: The requirements for and availability of analysis and verification methods and tools are an important factor in making architecture decisions. The system architect is responsible for selecting supporting methods and tools, just as they are responsible for selecting subsystems and components for the product itself. Technology should exist that allows the easy integration of selected development tools, just as technology should exist that allows the easy integration of selected system components. One goal of FASTAR is to enable easy integration of selected schedulability analysis tools.

We selected as our implementation platform the widelyused Eclipse-based Open Source AADL Tool Environment (OSATE) [18]. The interface between FASTAR and each selected analysis tool is implemented as an Eclipse plug-in. FASTAR provides an interface tailored for schedulability analysis plug-in development. The Eclipse Public License (EPL) together with Eclipse methods for modularizing and installing plug-ins supports our goal of an open framework that allows third-party integration of back-end analysis tools with their desired intellectual property rights.

Different parts of an AADL model are translated into the native input formats of the back-end schedulability analysis tools. There are dependencies between these multiple toolspecific models, e.g. a task hosted on a processor analyzed by one tool may send messages over networks that are analyzed by other tools. The framework extracts analysis results from some tools when generating input models for others. Because there may be cyclic dependencies between different parts of the system model, analysis must be performed iteratively until global convergence is achieved [14], [9]. The final analysis results from the different tools must be combined to check end-to-end timing requirements specified in the AADL system model.

Different schedulability theories model streams of timed events (such as arrival times for a sequence of messages received at an input port) in different ways. For example, a common event stream model for busy period analysis is a strictly periodic event sequence modified with jitter and offset parameters. In contrast, network calculi consider the maximum number of events that occur in time intervals of given lengths, specified using traffic functions α(t) that give the maximum number of possible arrivals in any time interval of length t.

If an AADL system model is decomposed so that a part of the system analyzed using a busy period approach sends events to a part of the system analyzed using a network calculus, then it is necessary to convert the output event stream model from the former to an input event stream model of the latter. As an example, consider a system model where a periodically dispatched thread on a processor sends a message over a switched Ethernet. Assume the thread dispatches are modeled as a sequence of strictly periodic events. A busy period analysis will result in a departure event model that has the same period but with jitter and offset due to thread execution time and contention with other threads. If the switched Ethernet is modeled and analyzed using a network calculus, then the message departure event model obtained from busy period analysis must be converted to a traffic arrival curve in the network calculus model. This is illustrated in Figure 3.

When back-end models are first generated, there are no analysis results for event stream flows that cross between models. The framework must select initial values. The initially generated models are analyzed to produce an initial set of analysis results. Models are generated again, this time using the available analysis results to better model event stream flows that cross between models. This iterative cycle of back-end model generation and analysis is repeated until a global fixed point for all analysis results is reached. The method of selecting initial values combined with monotonicity properties of the individual analyzers must be used to show that convergence will occur [14], [9]. Figure 4 shows a flow chart for overall compositional analysis.

div.head: IV. STATUS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: We have integrated two existing schedulability analysis tools into our initial FASTAR configuration, MAST[17] and SPICA [15]. We have applied this to several distributed system test cases (e.g. switched Ethernet and ARINC 653 modules). All these converged within seconds after at most 3 global iterations. However, only periodic workloads were modeled, and the largest workload only had about ten threads. More application experience, stress testing, and assessment of tightness of bounds is needed.
For a given set of analysis algorithms, event stream models, and event stream conversion algorithms, we want Fig. 3.

Event stream models of different tools need to be converted (portions from "Combined Approach to System Level Performance Analysis of Embedded Systems" [14]) Fig. 4. FASTAR flow chart some assurance that global iteration will converge [14]. This can be argued using monotonicity properties of analysis and conversion algorithms [9]. We need to collect, develop and document monotonicity results and convergence arguments for our currently integrated tools and supported protocols. New cases will need to be added as new event stream models and analysis and conversion algorithms are integrated into the framework.

Utilization budgeting and analysis is often used to manage early development. FASTAR includes a tool for utilization analysis of conceptual architecture specifications based on MIPS, BPS, and memory demand and supply. This tool (and some schedulability analysis tools) provides parametric sensitivity analysis for some model input parameters. It is possible to automate traceability and verification of initial utilization budgets against more detailed utilization models and schedulability analysis results as they become available.
There are a number of potential extensions to increase support for heterogeneous modeling and analysis.

In the current framework, all software hosted on a designated subset of resources is analyzed by the same designated tool. It would be desirable to also allow partitioning of the software workload on the same resource. For example, soft real-time event-driven client-server applications might be excluded from an analysis performed on hard real-time periodic and sporadic workloads. This would require some mixture of scheduling and analysis methods to bound and model the interference between the two workloads [3], [6].

Schedulability analysis and simulation are synergistic. Compositional simulation is a mature technology that could be added to the framework [23]. Once this is done, it would be possible to support hybrid analysis in which parts of the model are analyzed using simulation and parts analyzed using schedulability tools.

Mixed-analysis methods have also been demonstrated that allow computationally challenging techniques such as timed automata to be used for small subsystems within a more tractable analysis paradigm for the overall system [4].
